column1: # topic: Chapter 6: Imperial Triumph, Imperial Crisis, 1754-1776

column2: George Washington led Virginia militia to the forks of the Ohio, where his ambush killed Jumonville, and then surrendered Fort Necessity to the French.
Tanaghrisson was the Iroquois representative who killed the wounded Jumonville to set the French and British against each other for Iroquois interests.
Edward Braddock was the British general who alienated Indian allies and was killed when French and Indian sharpshooters ambushed his army in 1755.
William Pitt took over the war, had Britain pay for it and respect colonial militias, and won Indian allies, turning defeat into victory.
James Wolfe was the British general who took Quebec by scaling the bluffs to the Plains of Abraham and died in the battle.
Montcalm was the effective French commander who took key British forts and died defending Quebec.
Jeffery Amherst was the top British officer who cut off presents and diplomacy to Indians, helping provoke Pontiac's Rebellion, and was recalled.
Neolin was a Delaware holy man who preached that the Master of Life wanted Indians to drive out the British and return to tradition.
Pontiac was the Ottawa chief who embraced Neolin's message and led the 1763 attacks that captured British forts west of Detroit.
The Paxton Boys were Scots-Irish vigilantes in western Pennsylvania who murdered Christian Indians, including some in protective custody.
George Grenville was the treasury head who passed the Sugar, Currency, Quartering and Stamp Acts to make colonists help pay for the empire.
Patrick Henry was a young Virginia Burgess who introduced the Virginia Resolves denying Parliament's right to tax.
The Sons of Liberty were traders, lawyers and prosperous artisans who organized seaport crowds to intimidate stamp distributors and customs collectors.
Rockingham replaced Grenville and, backed by London merchants hurt by nonimportation, got the Stamp Act repealed.
Charles Townshend was the chancellor of the exchequer who passed the 1767 Townshend Acts.
John Dickinson wrote the widely read Letters from a Farmer in Pennsylvania urging colonists to buy fewer English luxuries.
Samuel Adams was a Massachusetts master organizer who sent the circular letter, started the committees of correspondence, and helped lead resistance in Boston.
The Daughters of Liberty were women who wore homespun, served coffee instead of tea, and boycotted shops selling British goods.
John Adams was a defense lawyer for the soldiers tried after the Boston Massacre.
Lord North repealed all Townshend duties except tea and then passed the Coercive Acts.
Thomas Gage was the British general and Massachusetts governor whose march to seize arms at Concord started the fighting.
Paul Revere carried the Suffolk Resolves to Congress and rode out to warn that the British were marching toward Concord.
Thomas Paine was an English-born former corsetmaker who wrote Common Sense in 1776.
